seoTitle: 1975 Oldsmobile Hurst Edition Preview: Running After Years Sitting | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: A sneak preview of a 1975 Oldsmobile Hurst Edition running again after sitting for many years — with notes from Dan Fitzgerald and the companion first-start clip of the same car.
guide:
Not every video needs to be a two-hour build to earn a look. This one is a sneak preview — and the star is a 1975 Oldsmobile Hurst Edition, running again after sitting for many years.

That's the whole story here, and I'll keep this page as honest as the video is short. Kenley calls it a sneak preview of what's coming: this car, awake after a long sleep, with more to come on it and the others in the shop.

There's a particular sound a big Oldsmobile makes when it clears its throat after years of sitting. If you know, you know.

## What the Video Covers

**A first look at the car.** A 1975 Oldsmobile Hurst Edition — one of the Hurst/Olds cars that carried the Hurst name into the mid-seventies — presented as a preview rather than a build episode.

**It runs.** The headline is simple: after sitting for many years, the car is running. That single fact changes everything about a project. A car that runs can be evaluated, sorted and planned around in a way a silent one can't.

**More to come.** Kenley promises more on this car and others. On this site, the next chapter already exists: the companion clip below catches this same Hurst Edition's first start.

## Key Takeaways

- A car that sat for years isn't automatically a parts car. Hearing it run is the first real data point in any revival.
- Previews are the "before" picture. Judge a project by where it starts, not just where it ends up.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

None to report yet — this is a first look, not a wrenching session. When the Hurst/Olds gets its full episodes, the details will land here.

## Keep Learning

If a long-sitting car has you tempted, [Buying Your First Classic Car](/post/buying-your-first-classic-car) covers how to judge one with your head instead of your heart, and [Winter Storage Done Right](/post/winter-storage-done-right) shows what good storage looks like — the thing that decides whether a car wakes up easy or hard after years away.

And watch this car take its next step in the [1975 Oldsmobile Hurst Edition first start](/how-to-videos/1975-oldsmobile-hurst-edition-first-start) clip.

title: Arizona Survivor GTO: What Sandblasting exposed- Rust & damage ( episode 2)
creator: Kenley's Car Stories

seoTitle: Sandblasting a Classic Car: What It Revealed on a 1971 GTO | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: See what sandblasting uncovered on an Arizona-survivor 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 — the rust and damage hiding under old paint and filler — with Dan Fitzgerald's written guide and takeaways for your own restoration.
guide:
Every restoration has a moment of truth, and for a lot of cars it happens in the blasting booth.

This is Episode 2 of Kenley's Car Stories' Ragged Out to Restored series. The car is a 1971 Pontiac GTO — factory 455 big block, Turbo Hydramatic, and a body that spent decades in the dry Arizona desert. By survivor standards it was billed as remarkably rust-free. Then it went to sandblasting, and the old paint stopped telling stories and the metal started.

That's why this episode earned a page here. Blasting is where a restoration stops being guesswork.

## What the Video Covers

**Finishing the teardown.** Before any blasting, the panel removal gets finished. Blasting works on a stripped shell — everything that can hide rust or trap media has to come off first.

**Off to the blasters.** The GTO goes out for sandblasting — the shop is AZ Blasting, linked in Kenley's description — to uncover what lies under the old paint. Decades of paint and filler can look straight and solid right up until the media hits them.

**What the bare metal said.** Rust and damage that were hiding under the old finish — on a car that had every excuse to be clean. If a dry-climate survivor can hide surprises, any car can. This is the segment that resets the restoration plan, because now the plan is based on evidence instead of hope.

**The detailed walk-around.** After blasting, Kenley does a detailed walk around the car. Don't skip this part. The walk-around is where findings become a work list: what gets repaired, what gets replaced, and in what order.

## Key Takeaways

- You don't know a classic car's body until it's in bare metal. Whatever the paint claims, blasting is the verification.
- "Rust-free" is a description, not a measurement. This Arizona car was remarkably clean for its age — and still had rust and damage hiding underneath.
- The walk-around afterward matters as much as the blasting. Findings only help if they turn into a documented plan.
- Strip in the right order: panels off first, then blast. Media finds every crevice you leave assembled.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

This step isn't about parts — it's about a process. The car goes to a professional blasting shop rather than being blasted in the driveway, and the teardown ahead of it is hand-tool work: unbolting panels and keeping track of what came from where. The most important tool in this episode is a camera and a notebook during the walk-around. What you document in bare metal is what your budget and your body man will work from.

## Keep Learning

What happens next is the subject of [Classic Car Paint Preparation](/post/classic-car-paint-preparation) — stripping is only the start; repair, blocking and primer decide the finish. And because blasting surprises have a way of rewriting budgets, [How to Build a Classic Car Restoration Budget That Actually Works](/post/how-to-build-a-classic-car-restoration-budget-that-actually-works) is the other essential read before you start a teardown of your own.

Follow this same GTO forward: Episode 4 is the [Vintage Air installation](/how-to-videos/vintage-air-installation-firewall-engine-prep-plus-engine-core-support-install), and Episode 5 is the [Holley Sniper 2 & HyperSpark guide](/how-to-videos/holley-sniper-2-hyperspark-guide-plus-vintage-air-wiring). The build just keeps getting more honest.

title: Vintage Air installation: Firewall & Engine prep (plus engine & core support install)
creator: Kenley's Car Stories
recommendation: Especially relevant for restorers installing modern A/C in a classic car, with useful firewall and engine-bay preparation details.
seoTitle: Vintage Air Installation Guide: Firewall & Engine Prep — 1971 GTO | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: Watch a Vintage Air install on a 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 — firewall prep and seam sealing, HVAC box and hoses, engine and accessory install, compressor and condenser — with Dan Fitzgerald's written guide and key takeaways.
guide:
Adding air conditioning to a classic car sounds like a single job. It isn't. It's a dozen jobs wearing a trench coat.

That's the honest lesson of this video from Kenley's Car Stories. It's Episode 4 of his 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 restoration, and while the Vintage Air HVAC box and hoses do get installed, Kenley is upfront that the process is not linear. The firewall has to be modified and painted first. The frame and core support need cleaning and paint. The engine and transmission go in along the way. The air conditioning rides on top of all of it.

If you're planning a Vintage Air install in your own car, this is the episode that shows you what the job actually looks like — in the right order, with the detours left in.

## What the Video Covers

**Starting at the firewall.** The original HVAC comes out and the firewall gets prepared: a filler panel goes in, seams get sealed, and the firewall and frame are sanded and painted while everything is still out of the way. This is the part of an A/C install nobody brags about, and it's the part that decides how the finished job looks.

**The Vintage Air box and hoses.** With the firewall ready, the HVAC box and hoses go in. Real builds involve substitutions, and this one is no exception — Kenley runs a 3/4-inch heater hose where a 5/8 was expected. Afterward he does something more builders should copy: an on-camera debrief of how the box installation went.

**Core support and front-end cleanup.** The core support gets cleaned and painted, the wheel liners get undercoated, and the headers get wrapped. Unglamorous work, done while the access is easy.

**Engine and supporting systems.** A replacement starter from Jegs goes in — and then needs a spacer to get the setback right. The engine is installed, with a moment where it sits crooked and has to be sorted out. The power steering hoses are rebuilt, the pump, pulley and brackets follow, and the Powermaster alternator gets re-clocked and modified to fit the plan.

**Compressor, condenser and supports.** The Vintage Air compressor goes on, the radiator support is installed with new bushings, and the condenser is assembled and installed. One honest note from Kenley: the system still gets its final completion once the body comes back from paint. Restoration is sequencing, and he doesn't pretend otherwise.

## Key Takeaways

- An A/C install is sequenced, not linear. Firewall, paint, engine and accessories all gate the HVAC work — plan for the detours instead of being surprised by them.
- Do firewall work while everything is out. Seam sealing and paint are easy now and miserable after the box is mounted.
- Expect substitutions. A different hose size, a starter that needs a spacer — real builds adapt, and the fix is usually simple once you see it.
- Debrief your own work. Kenley stops and reviews how the box install went before moving on. That habit catches problems while they're still cheap.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

The headliner is the Vintage Air system itself — HVAC box, hoses, compressor and condenser. Around it: a firewall filler panel, seam sealer, a starter from Jegs with a spacer, a Powermaster alternator, fresh radiator support bushings and header wrap. No single hero tool here. The hero is the order of operations.

## Keep Learning

This episode pairs with the next one: in the [Holley Sniper 2 & HyperSpark guide](/how-to-videos/holley-sniper-2-hyperspark-guide-plus-vintage-air-wiring), Kenley wires this same Vintage Air system into the car. And if you want to see where this GTO started, Episode 2 is the [sandblasting episode](/how-to-videos/arizona-survivor-gto-what-sandblasting-exposed-rust-damage-episode-2), where bare metal told the truth about the body.

On the article side, the HVAC box lives behind the dash, so [Dash Restoration: Where a Classic Car Comes Back to Life](/post/dash-restoration-where-a-classic-car-comes-back-to-life) covers the interior half of this same territory. The firewall work here is paint prep in miniature — [Classic Car Paint Preparation](/post/classic-car-paint-preparation) explains why the finish is only as good as what lies beneath. And when accessories and wiring start multiplying, [Classic Car Electrical Troubleshooting](/post/classic-car-electrical-troubleshooting) is the process that keeps you sane.

title: Holley Sniper 2 & Hyperspark Guide ( plus Vintage Air Wiring)
creator: Kenley's Car Stories

seoTitle: Holley Sniper 2 EFI Install & Wiring Guide — 1971 GTO | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: Watch a complete Holley Sniper 2 and HyperSpark install on a 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 — custom battery cables, fuse block, Vintage Air wiring and a no-start diagnosis — with Dan Fitzgerald's written guide, key steps and takeaways.
guide:
Most EFI conversions don't fail on the fuel injection. They fail on the wiring.

That's why this video from Kenley's Car Stories earned a full page here. It's Episode 5 of his 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 restoration, and in just over two hours Kenley installs a Holley Sniper 2 with a HyperSpark distributor, builds the car's power distribution from scratch, wires in his Vintage Air, and then chases down a no-start that turns out to be his own wiring mistake. He shows all of it, including the mistake. That's the kind of video worth studying.

## What the Video Covers

**Getting the Sniper 2 and HyperSpark in place.** The opening stretch covers mounting the EFI unit, installing the HyperSpark distributor, setting timing to top dead center, and deciding where the Holley controller and modules will live.

**Building wires and power distribution.** Kenley builds his MSD 8mm spark plug wires by hand, makes custom battery cables, and adds an underhood fuse block. Before any of it goes to work, he checks the new cables for continuity and resistance.

**The "Nerd Corner."** My favorite part. Kenley slows down and shows how to diagnose high-resistance terminals with a digital volt-ohm meter. A connection can look perfectly fine and still steal voltage. This segment shows how to prove it with a meter instead of guessing.

**Marrying the new system to the old car.** Rather than ripping out the factory wiring, he simplifies the original engine harness and keeps what the car still needs — oil pressure and temperature. The Vintage Air wiring and firewall bulkhead connector go in during this stretch, along with the heater hoses.

**Fuel delivery.** An in-tank fuel pump install, the tank going back in, fuel filter placement, and the wide-band oxygen sensor the Sniper needs in order to learn.

**First power-up — and a no-start.** Software downloads, firmware updates, and the initial settings all go fine. Then the fuel pump won't run. Kenley works the problem on camera and finds it: a wiring mistake in how the power distribution module and a relay were connected — his own error, shown and explained before he fixes it.

**First start.** The 455 fires for the first time in over four months. He finishes by tidying up the wiring, vacuum-filling the cooling system, and checking timing and idle.

## Key Takeaways

- Test new cables before you trust them. A few minutes with a meter on the bench beats hours of guessing under the hood.
- Keep the factory circuits the car still needs. Simplifying a harness is not the same thing as removing it.
- A no-start is usually one wrong connection, not a bad system. The fix in this video came from methodical checking, not new parts.
- Even experienced builders mis-wire something now and then. What matters is having a process that finds it.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

The featured hardware is the Holley Sniper 2 EFI system with the HyperSpark distributor and controller, hand-built MSD 8mm plug wires, an underhood fuse block, custom battery cables, Vintage Air, and an in-tank fuel pump. The tool doing the quiet hero work, though, is a plain digital multimeter.

If your meter is a bargain-bin special that reads a little differently every time you touch the probes, this is the job that will expose it. The meter I recommend in my Garage is the [Fluke 117 True-RMS Digital Multimeter](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Fluke+117+Digital+Multimeter&tag=fitzgeraldcla-20) — the kind of buy-it-once tool that makes a test like Kenley's high-resistance check worth trusting.

*Disclosure: the Fluke link above is an affiliate link. If you buy through it, Fitzgerald Classics earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.*

## Keep Learning

Wiring a build like this one leans on the same fundamentals I wrote about in [Classic Car Electrical Troubleshooting](/post/classic-car-electrical-troubleshooting) — find the fault before you replace parts. If you're testing components off the car, [Bench Testing Classic-Car Electrical Components](/post/bench-testing-classic-car-electrical-components-without-destroying-them) walks through doing it safely, and [7 Electrical Tools Every Classic-Car Owner Should Have](/post/7-electrical-tools-every-classic-car-owner-should-have) covers the rest of the kit.

title: Repairing Door Hinges.. It's pretty easy! 1971 Pontiac GTO ragged out to restoed series video.
creator: Kenley's Car Stories

seoTitle: GM A-Body Door Hinge Rebuild — 1971 GTO | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: Watch a door hinge rebuild on a 1971 Pontiac GTO — a process that works for most 1970s through 1990s GM cars and trucks — with Dan Fitzgerald's written guide, key steps and takeaways.
guide:
Doors that sag, scrape and refuse to line up are usually not a door problem. They're a hinge problem — and on a lot of classic GM cars, the fix is a rebuild, not a replacement.

In this video from Kenley's Car Stories, the door hinges on his 1971 Pontiac GTO get a full refresh. Kenley's own title for the job says it plainly: it's pretty easy. This is one of those satisfying repairs — a modest job that changes how the whole car feels every time you open and close the door.

Shorter video, shorter page. But if you own a GM car or truck from this era, this one earns its place here.

## What the Video Covers

**The job itself.** A complete rebuild of a set of 1970s GM A-body door hinges, done on the GTO as the car moves from ragged survivor to refreshed driver. Worn hinges let a heavy door drop and wander; a rebuild refreshes the original hardware instead of replacing it.

**Why it travels well.** Kenley points out that this same process works for most 1970s through 1990s GM cars and trucks — the Chevelle crowd included. A-body hinges of this era share their basic design across a wide range of GM iron, so the lesson isn't limited to one Pontiac.

**Where it fits in the build.** This is series work: the same car that got stripped and blasted earlier in the build. Kenley flags the next step after the hinges as body and paint — which is exactly right. Doors have to hang true before paint, not after.

## Key Takeaways

- Sagging doors are usually worn hinge pins and bushings, not a bent door or a bad hinge. A rebuild refreshes the originals.
- Rebuilding keeps your factory hinges — the ones that fit your car — instead of gambling on reproductions. I make the same case in the article linked below.
- Sequence matters: hinges before paint. Aligning doors after the car is painted is a good way to chip the paint you're aligning.
- One process covers a lot of iron: most '70s through '90s GM cars and trucks share this hinge design.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

The parts side of this job is a door hinge pin and bushing kit for GM A-bodies. The tool that earns its keep is whatever drives the old pins out — and that's a step where a steel punch can slip and scar the hinge or the door edge. Brass is softer than the hinge steel, so a brass drift moves the pin without chewing things up. The set I recommend in my Garage is the [Mayhew Pro Brass Drift Punch Set](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Mayhew+Pro+brass+drift+punch+set&tag=fitzgeraldcla-20).

*Disclosure: the Mayhew link above is an affiliate link. If you buy through it, Fitzgerald Classics earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.*

## Keep Learning

Door fit is a bigger topic than one hinge, and I wrote the companion piece: [Classic Car Body Panel Alignment](/post/classic-car-body-panel-alignment) explains why gaps tell the story of a restoration and why hinge and structure problems get diagnosed before paint. The rebuild-versus-replace question behind this job is the whole subject of [Restore It or Replace It?](/post/restore-it-or-replace-it), and since body and paint come next in Kenley's series, [Classic Car Paint Preparation](/post/classic-car-paint-preparation) is the right follow-up read.

More on this same car: the [sandblasting episode](/how-to-videos/arizona-survivor-gto-what-sandblasting-exposed-rust-damage-episode-2) shows what bare metal revealed, the [Holley Sniper 2 guide](/how-to-videos/holley-sniper-2-hyperspark-guide-plus-vintage-air-wiring) is the series' big wiring-and-EFI episode, and there's a quick companion [door hinge Short](/how-to-videos/71gm-door-hinges-rebuild-pontiac-gto) covering the same job in short form.
